prompt: Create a Steal a Brainrot style multiplayer Roblox game. Preserve its recognizable core loop. Use original procedural characters and UI, no uploaded assets or monetization. Choose sensible defaults, ask no questions. Plan a feasible first playable slice and explicitly state what is deferred.

spec.title: Snatchling Showdown — First Playable Slice
spec.summary:
Build an original, session-based multiplayer tycoon/raiding game inside the Forge_PlanningBenchmark namespace. The recognizable loop is preserved: players receive a personal base and starter cash, purchase visible income-producing creatures from a shared central conveyor, reinvest passive income, contest creatures while they travel, protect their collection with a timed shield, steal exposed creatures from rivals, counter thieves with a telegraphed shove, and rebirth for a lasting session bonus.

Sensible first-slice defaults: eight single-floor bases; $100 starting cash; six producer slots per base; Common, Uncommon, and Rare offers; a new conveyor offer every 6 seconds; automatic income ticks once per second; 30 seconds of join protection; a 45-second manually activated shield followed by a 60-second cooldown; one carried creature per thief; reduced carry WalkSpeed; and a first rebirth requiring $2,500 plus three owned creatures. Rebirth resets cash and creatures, increments a session rebirth count, grants +25% income per rebirth, and adds 5 seconds to manual shield duration.

Contested acquisition is adapted into a clear prototype rule: until an offer reaches a base, another player may pay its displayed takeover price to become the claimant. Each successful takeover multiplies the next price by 1.5, and previous payments are not refunded. Delivery finalizes ownership if the claimant has capacity; otherwise the offer remains contestable or eventually despawns with a documented server-side resolution.

The project uses only Parts, constraints/joints, built-in materials, text, gradients, particles, highlights, and permitted Roblox stock sound paths. Creatures, icons, map dressing, animations, and UI are generated procedurally; no uploaded images, meshes, animations, or audio IDs are required. There are no developer products, passes, paid escapes, premium boosts, purchase prompts, or other monetization.

Deferred beyond the first playable slice: cross-server/DataStore persistence; trading; additional base floors; more than six slots; elaborate gear inventories; damage-based combat; multiple attack types; NPC pathfinding around complex obstacles; traits, mutations, Lucky Blocks, timed rare guarantees, live events, seasonal content, quests, global leaderboards, matchmaking, social rewards, custom uploaded music or voice, localization, and production-scale analytics/moderation tooling. Monetization is excluded rather than deferred. Exact tuning from the reference is intentionally not copied because retrieved sources disagree or are unofficial; the stated prototype values are original defaults. Rebirth bonuses persist through death and respawn but, until persistence is implemented, do not survive leaving the server.
spec.visualDirection:
Use a bright, toy-like industrial arena with eight color-coded bases arranged around a shared central runway. The marketplace is a red-orange moving-belt illusion made from animated floor strips and chevrons, with large overhead signs showing that it is the shared acquisition zone. Bases use chunky geometric walls, six illuminated display pads, a prominent shield button, a translucent gate, and highly readable owner, shield, and capacity labels.

The collectible cast is an original family of “Snatchlings”: absurd but non-derivative creatures assembled from primitive Parts with contrasting proportions, stalk eyes, block feet, antennae, fins, or spring-like limbs. Each rarity has a coherent procedural palette and silhouette treatment rather than copied meme characters. Offers display an original generated name, rarity, current price, and cash-per-second rate in a BillboardGui. Idle producers bob, blink, and sway; conveyor offers waddle with alternating procedural leg motion; claimed offers lean toward their destination; carried creatures visibly attach behind the thief.

UI uses original text-only symbols and geometric panels—no image assets. The HUD prioritizes cash, income per second, base capacity, shield status/cooldown, rebirth progress, and short event alerts. Green communicates earnings and safe ownership, amber communicates contestable transit, cyan communicates active shielding, and red communicates theft or danger. Mobile controls use a large contextual shove button, while keyboard/mouse and gamepad receive matching prompts. Effects remain lightweight: highlights, pulses, particles, color flashes, camera shake, and stock sound cues only.

requirements.description: Run a shared central conveyor that continuously presents procedurally generated offers with visible rarity, price, and income rate.
requirements.acceptance: The server spawns one offer approximately every 6 seconds from a configured Common/Uncommon/Rare table; every offer has readable labels, traverses the central runway, can be purchased through a device-compatible prompt, and is cleaned up at the route end or timeout.

requirements.description: Owned Snatchlings occupy finite base slots and automatically generate server-authoritative cash.
requirements.acceptance: Each base has six visible slots; delivered producers occupy individual slots; the server credits their configured combined rate once per second with rebirth multiplier applied; cash and income displays update without relying on client-reported values.

requirements.description: Keep purchased conveyor offers contestable until they arrive at the current claimant's base.
requirements.acceptance: A claimed offer visibly travels toward its claimant's base. Another eligible player can pay the current takeover price to redirect it; each takeover raises the next price by 1.5, charges the new claimant without refunding prior buyers, updates labels and destination for all clients, and finalizes ownership only on valid delivery.

requirements.description: Allow players to take one producer from an unshielded enemy base and capture it by carrying it into their own base.
requirements.acceptance: A server-validated prompt is available only for a rival producer in an unshielded base and within interaction distance. Successful pickup removes it from its slot, visibly attaches it to the thief, and transfers it only when the living carrier reaches their own capture zone with free capacity.

requirements.description: Make theft an exposed carry state with movement penalty, owner alerts, and a counterattack that returns the producer.
requirements.acceptance: A carrier is visibly marked, has reduced server-controlled WalkSpeed, cannot pick up another producer, and triggers an immediate alert for the owner. A valid shove from another player returns the producer to its prior owner and slot or a valid fallback slot; carrier death, reset, disconnect, or invalid destination also resolves the producer without duplication or loss.

requirements.description: Give every owner a readable timed base shield that blocks theft and hostile entry while active.
requirements.acceptance: New owners receive 30 seconds of protection. The owner can activate a 45-second shield, plus 5 seconds per rebirth, when off cooldown; a 60-second cooldown begins after expiry. Gate visuals and replicated timer state clearly communicate active, expiring, and cooldown states. Server checks prevent hostile entry and theft while allowing the owner to leave.

requirements.description: Provide a single repeatable rebirth action that resets short-term economy in exchange for session-long economic and defense bonuses.
requirements.acceptance: At $2,500 and three owned producers, the player can confirm rebirth. The server removes owned and carried producers, resets cash to $100, increments rebirth count, applies +25% income and +5 seconds of shield duration per count, preserves the count across character respawns, and communicates that cross-server persistence is deferred.

requirements.description: Implement actual counterplay with visible anticipation, active, hit-reaction, and recovery phases using procedural character joints.
requirements.acceptance: Keyboard/mouse, touch, and gamepad can request a shove. The server enforces living state, rate limit, phase state, range, facing, and target validity. The move has about 0.25 seconds of readable wind-up, a brief active check, and about 0.5 seconds of recovery; shoulder/torso Motor6D movement is visible, a successful carrier hit produces knockback or stagger feedback and returns the stolen producer, and misses still complete recovery.

requirements.description: Provide persistent, device-responsive HUD and notifications for the complete loop.
requirements.acceptance: A ResetOnSpawn=false ScreenGui displays cash, income rate, slots, shield timer/cooldown, rebirth count/requirements, contextual controls, purchase failures, successful income/delivery, contest changes, theft alerts, and return outcomes. It reads initial replicated state, observes later changes, survives respawn without duplicate connections, and scales for desktop, mobile, and console safe areas.

requirements.description: Provide lightweight procedural visual and audible feedback without uploaded assets.
requirements.acceptance: Purchases, deliveries, shield activation, theft, and shove hits have distinct visible effects. Audible cues may use only documented built-in paths such as rbxasset://sounds/action_jump.mp3, rbxasset://sounds/action_jump_land.mp3, and rbxasset://sounds/action_falling.ogg; no custom music is claimed, and cue volume/pitch variations remain understandable without being required for gameplay.

requirements.description: Keep economy, ownership, combat, protection, and rebirth authoritative and validated on the server.
requirements.acceptance: Clients send only action intent. The server independently checks player identity, assigned base, humanoid health, distance, capacity, balances, ownership, shield state, carry state, action phase, and per-action rate limits. Remote names and payload shapes are centralized, malformed requests fail safely, and clients cannot directly award cash or transfer producers.

requirements.description: Handle assignment, respawn, disconnects, and cleanup without affecting unrelated place objects.
requirements.acceptance: Up to eight players receive distinct bases. Character respawn restores movement and bindings without duplicating state. Leaving releases the base, destroys only that player's session objects, disconnects listeners, and safely resolves carried or owned producers. All static and dynamic instances remain under supplied Forge_PlanningBenchmark roots, and unrelated place content is not destroyed.

referenceDecisions.reason: The shared, visible marketplace is essential to the recognizable acquisition loop. The slice uses original Snatchlings, original tuning, and device-compatible prompts rather than copied characters or presentation.
Automatic producer income and reinvestment form the tycoon half of the core loop and are fully included with six finite slots.

Because retrieved sources do not establish an authoritative formula, the prototype uses an explicit server-authoritative takeover rule: each new claimant pays the displayed price, prior buyers receive no refund, and the next takeover price rises by 1.5 until delivery.
Entering an exposed rival base, carrying out one producer, and delivering it home is retained as the primary active multiplayer objective.

The vulnerable carry state, slowdown, visible attachment, owner alert, and return-on-counterattack are retained. Broad gear combat is narrowed to one original, readable shove so the first slice has actual fair counterplay without an oversized combat inventory.

Timed owner-controlled protection is retained with original, clearly stated values: 30-second join protection, 45-second activation, and 60-second cooldown. Server gate enforcement replaces uncertain reference-specific trapping behavior.
A repeatable reset with income and shield bonuses is included to complete the long-term loop, but the first slice keeps it session-scoped until DataStore persistence is implemented and verified.

research.summary: Steal a Brainrot is described by the retrieved evidence as a multiplayer tycoon/PvP game built around acquiring income-producing collectible characters, defending them at a personal base, and stealing them from other players. A shared central conveyor continuously presents characters with visible prices, rarities, and earning rates. Purchased characters travel toward the buyer’s base, where they generate passive cash that funds stronger purchases. Rival players can contest characters in transit or enter an unprotected base, carry a character home, and claim it. Temporary base locks, theft penalties, owner alerts, and gear-based counterplay turn otherwise idle progression into a recurring risk/reward cycle. Rebirth resets short-term wealth and collections in exchange for permanent economic, capacity, defense, or equipment benefits. The clearest independent account is Kotaku’s gameplay description; the wiki, Game Devourer, and PlayXArena are secondary community/guide sources. No original Roblox experience listing or creator documentation was included in the retrieved pages, so precise statistics and tuning should not be treated as authoritative. The recognizable loop supported by multiple sources is: acquire a producer, wait for passive income, reinvest in better producers, expose or secure the collection through timed defenses, raid competitors, recover from losses, and eventually rebirth for permanent progression.

mechanics.description: A central shared conveyor or red-carpet marketplace continuously introduces collectible characters. Each offer communicates at least its price, rarity, and income rate. A player with enough cash can purchase an offer, after which the character travels toward that player’s base. Because the marketplace is shared, acquisition is visible and contestable rather than a private shop transaction.

Owned characters occupy the player’s storage or base and repeatedly generate cash. Higher-rarity and more expensive characters generally produce more income, creating an idle-tycoon reinvestment loop in which earnings buy progressively stronger producers.

A character bought from the shared marketplace is not necessarily safe until it reaches the buyer’s base. Other players can attempt to redirect or buy it during transit, producing costly back-and-forth purchase contests. The community wiki additionally claims prices rise when players contest an offer, but that exact rule and its formula are not independently verified by the retrieved evidence.

Players may enter an enemy base while its protection is inactive, pick up one of its income-producing characters, and carry it back to their own base. Successful delivery transfers a valuable economic asset, allowing risky theft to substitute for lengthy saving and making every accumulated collection a multiplayer objective.

Stealing creates a vulnerable carry state. The community wiki reports that the thief moves much more slowly, loses access to items, visibly carries the stolen character, and triggers an immediate owner notification. Other players can attack the carrier to return the character. These consequences turn theft into an exposed escape attempt rather than an instant transfer.

Each base has a temporary lock or shield activated by its owner. While active, it prevents hostile entry while still allowing the owner to leave, enabling both defensive timing and opportunistic raids. Once protection expires, the collection becomes vulnerable. Retrieved sources mention initial join protection and approximately 60-second activations, but the exact duration, cooldown behavior, intruder trapping, and rebirth scaling require verification.

Rebirth is the long-term progression layer. After meeting resource or collection requirements, a player resets cash, owned characters, and some upgrades in exchange for permanent advantages reportedly including income multipliers, extra capacity, longer defense timers, base improvements, and access to additional gear. This gives the repeated acquire-defend-steal loop a reset goal and accelerating progression.

Personal bases provide finite display or storage slots for income producers. The community wiki describes additional floors and slots unlocked through rebirth progression, with upper floors increasing the time required for a thief to reach and escape with valuable characters. Exact floor counts and thresholds are guide claims rather than independently confirmed rules.

The reported onboarding starts the player with a small cash balance, assigns a base, grants short initial protection, and directs the purchase of an inexpensive first producer. Marketplace labels, cash totals, income rates, rarity, lock timers, interaction prompts, and theft notifications are necessary presentation systems implied or directly described by the guides.

Characters are divided into rarity tiers that affect scarcity, price, and earning potential. The community wiki also describes timed rare spawns, event variants, traits or mutations, and Lucky Blocks that eventually yield a random character. These extend collection goals but are supplementary to the basic conveyor, income, defense, and theft loop.

unknowns: No original Roblox experience listing, creator documentation, or direct first-party gameplay evidence was present in the retrieved material; authorship, release date, platform statistics, and record claims remain unverified.

The exact current starting cash, first-character price and income, base capacity, rarity table, spawn probabilities, and progression costs may have changed and should not be copied as authoritative tuning.
Sources are inconsistent or incomplete about initial protection versus repeatable shield duration, whether a cooldown exists, and exactly when the owner may reactivate protection.
The precise contested-purchase algorithm is unclear, including who receives the character, whether every click raises its price, whether spent money is refunded, and when ownership becomes final.

The exact theft interaction, valid targets, carry speed reduction, item restrictions, owner notification behavior, hit rules, invulnerability windows, and conditions for returning or transferring a character are not independently verified.

The available text does not establish authoritative visual specifications for the map, bases, laser gates, conveyor, character silhouettes, animation timing, UI typography, color palette, effects, or sounds beyond broad descriptions such as red conveyor and voxel-style meme creatures.
Rebirth requirements, reset scope, multiplier values, slot unlock thresholds, lock-time bonuses, and permanent gear unlocks are only described broadly or by a fan wiki and may vary by update.

Lucky Blocks, event schedules, mutations, traits, rare-spawn guarantees, extra base floors, and specialized gear appear to be later supporting systems rather than requirements of the minimum recognizable core loop.
The supplied YouTube page contains only a short transcript fragment and does not establish that the full video was watched or verify the implementation shown.

Claims about paid escape options and Robux purchases describe the reference but are unnecessary to its mechanical identity; their exact behavior and current availability are not verified by the retrieved first-party evidence.

spec.title: Steal a Brainrot Style Multiplayer Roblox Game
spec.summary: This project plans a multiplayer Roblox game replicating the recognizable core loop of Steal a Brainrot. Players spawn as procedural humanoid characters with unique random visual traits, roam a shared arena, and attempt to steal 'brains' from others by approaching and triggering an interaction. Successful theft triggers immediate visual and sound feedback, and updates scoring in the HUD. The first playable slice includes: player procedural character generation, multiplayer spawn and state, basic movement, UI showing player name and score, a steal action proximity system for opponents, and detection/server validation of stealing events with scoring updates. Audio and visual effects for steal events and hit reactions appear. Player respawn after elimination is included to enable multiplayer rounds. The game uses no uploaded assets or monetization, only original procedural models, sounds using Roblox built-in assets, and UI made with built-in elements. Deferred features include detailed character animations beyond idle/move, complex AI or NPCs, progression and monetization systems, in-depth cosmetic customizations, game lobby/matchmaking, extensive HUD menus, and polish FX beyond basic feedback. The visual direction emphasizes colorful, blocky procedural characters distinct from Roblox defaults with visible brains, a bright arena environment, clear UI score and steal opportunity indicators, and crisp immediate effects on stealing to reinforce gameplay feedback.
spec.visualDirection: Characters are procedurally generated humanoids with simple geometry parts (blocks, spheres) and varied random colors forming bodies, limbs, and heads. The brain is a distinguishable colored sphere or object visible inside or atop the head. Environment is a bright, open arena with simple ground and walls. UI uses bold, clean fonts and simple colored bars or icons for player score and steal prompts. Stolen brain effects are a brief particle sparkle or glow on the victim and a sound from built-in Roblox assets. Characters use basic idle and movement poses with subtle procedural limb motion. Steal interaction proximity prompts appear as small UI icons above targets or on the screen corner. Overall visual goals are clarity, boldness, and distinctive avatars without uploaded textures or external assets.

Owned characters occupy the player’s storage or base and repeatedly generate cash. Higher-rarity and more expensive characters generally produce more income, creating an idle-tycoon reinvestment loop in which earnings buy progressively stronger producers.

A character bought from the shared marketplace is not necessarily safe until it reaches the buyer’s base. Other players can attempt to redirect or buy it during transit, producing costly back-and-forth purchase contests. The community wiki additionally claims prices rise when players contest an offer, but that exact rule and its formula are not independently verified by the retrieved evidence.

Players may enter an enemy base while its protection is inactive, pick up one of its income-producing characters, and carry it back to their own base. Successful delivery transfers a valuable economic asset, allowing risky theft to substitute for lengthy saving and making every accumulated collection a multiplayer objective.

Stealing creates a vulnerable carry state. The community wiki reports that the thief moves much more slowly, loses access to items, visibly carries the stolen character, and triggers an immediate owner notification. Other players can attack the carrier to return the character. These consequences turn theft into an exposed escape attempt rather than an instant transfer.

Each base has a temporary lock or shield activated by its owner. While active, it prevents hostile entry while still allowing the owner to leave, enabling both defensive timing and opportunistic raids. Once protection expires, the collection becomes vulnerable. Retrieved sources mention initial join protection and approximately 60-second activations, but the exact duration, cooldown behavior, intruder trapping, and rebirth scaling require verification.

Rebirth is the long-term progression layer. After meeting resource or collection requirements, a player resets cash, owned characters, and some upgrades in exchange for permanent advantages reportedly including income multipliers, extra capacity, longer defense timers, base improvements, and access to additional gear. This gives the repeated acquire-defend-steal loop a reset goal and accelerating progression.

Personal bases provide finite display or storage slots for income producers. The community wiki describes additional floors and slots unlocked through rebirth progression, with upper floors increasing the time required for a thief to reach and escape with valuable characters. Exact floor counts and thresholds are guide claims rather than independently confirmed rules.

The reported onboarding starts the player with a small cash balance, assigns a base, grants short initial protection, and directs the purchase of an inexpensive first producer. Marketplace labels, cash totals, income rates, rarity, lock timers, interaction prompts, and theft notifications are necessary presentation systems implied or directly described by the guides.

Characters are divided into rarity tiers that affect scarcity, price, and earning potential. The community wiki also describes timed rare spawns, event variants, traits or mutations, and Lucky Blocks that eventually yield a random character. These extend collection goals but are supplementary to the basic conveyor, income, defense, and theft loop.
